comments.author: @riffsoffov9291
comments.text:
"I'm tired of people pretending that economic and trade ties are enough to stop large scale conflict"
The belief goes back to at least 1909, when Norman Angell's book "The Great Illusion" was published. From Wikipedia:

Angell's primary thesis was, in the words of historian James Joll, that "the economic cost of war was so great that no one could possibly hope to gain by starting a war the consequences of which would be so disastrous."[4][5] For that reason, a general European war was very unlikely to start, and if it did, it would not last long.

Whether or not the book was propaganda aimed at Germany, as historian Niall Ferguson claims, it was very popular in Britain and apparently convinced many that war in Europe was impossible. The First World War started in 1914 and lasted four years.

comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
Recursive self-improvement will be pursued by virtually everyone who can pursue it.

Why?

For the same reason a 'pause' in AI development can't happen.

Somebody will pursue it, to gain advantage over everyone else. Including bad actors. Not pursuing self-improvement is to fall behind and let someone else dominate AI.

And dominate us.

We are already dominated, of course. We have our socioeconomic hierarchies, wealth distribution, political hierarchies, all of that. We are in constant competition with each other for positions within those hierarchies, and groups compete, too. Often enough, the competition is brutal. Deadly.

I am not a Palmer Lucky fan, but he makes half an interesting point about AI precision in weapons. Potential targets should feel fear.

The other half of that point is the implications for dominance. Would Putin attack Ukraine if Ukraine could pull a trigger and end him, precisely him? Who gains this capability can take domination to new heights. Wealth accumulation. Exploitation.

And that's just one aspect of the capabilities falling into very human hands.

I don't fear Skynet. I fear what humans will do.

But there is nothing that can be done to stop it. The best we can hope for is to distribute these capabilities widely enough to create checks and balances - we can't even guess what that will look like, but at least no single group hierarchy will emerge unchallenged. I think this is what is in Elon's mind when he agitates for open AI (not the company, the concept).

State actors will lust for control. That will play out soon, I think, not merely by developing autonomous weapons. A state is nothing if it does not enjoy a monopoly of force over its citizens. AI in private hands will be a bone of contention.
